title: Move the DNS server without anyone noticing
role: You run the only DNS server for an office, its servers and two Docker hosts: a Pi-hole v6 in Docker. It must move to a new machine, and nobody should notice.

source.label: Pi-hole forum: Moving pi-hole to another machine? (30 April 2025), with Pi-hole's docs

brief: The old Pi-hole at 192.0.2.53 answers every lookup on the network and also hands out DHCP leases. The new machine is ready at 192.0.2.54. There is no second resolver: any gap is felt by everyone. Each choice names its rung on the risk ladder.

steps.situation: You test a full backup import on the new server. Afterwards it answers nothing and logs a warning. Its only network interface is `ens18`.
steps.evidence:
$ docker exec pihole pihole-FTL --config dns.interface
eth0
$ ip -br link | grep -v lo
ens18            UP             52:54:00:12:34:56
DNSMASQ_WARN: interface eth0 does not currently exist

choices.text: Bring only lists, records and groups; pin interface, listening mode, DHCP and web port with FTLCONF_ variables
choices.why: Rung 5 on a server no client uses yet. Interface, listening mode and DHCP describe a machine, not your data. Pi-hole's docs say settings set by environment variable become read-only, so no later import can change them.

choices.text: Import everything again, then fix whatever breaks
choices.why: The same import brings the same machine settings. It is a second change on top of the first, with no new evidence.

choices.text: Copy the old `/etc/pihole` folder across as it is
choices.why: Fast, but it carries the old interface and DHCP settings too, plus a query database you do not need.

choices.text: Re-enter local records from an exported text file and compare
choices.why: Safe and checkable, only slower. It still needs the machine settings set on purpose.

steps.situation: People say DNS "stops" at busy times, and the dashboard shows a high load. Someone suggests a bigger box.
steps.evidence:
$ dig @192.0.2.53 registry.example.com | grep status
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: REFUSED, id: 4127
$ docker exec pihole df -h /dev/shm
Filesystem  Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
shm          64M   63M  1.0M  99% /dev/shm

choices.text: Read the FTL log for rate-limit and shared-memory lines; check /dev/shm
choices.why: Rung 1. Pi-hole answers REFUSED once a client passes 1000 queries in 60 seconds, and containers behind one Docker host all arrive from its one address. Docker's default 64 MB /dev/shm can fill up and stop FTL.

choices.text: Too many users: size the new machine up and move on
choices.why: A bigger box changes neither the per-client limit nor the shared-memory size. Inside a container the load figure is the host's anyway.
Rung 7 on the only resolver, as a habit. Each restart is a short outage and clears the state you needed to see.

steps.situation: The new server gives the same answers as the old one for every local name. How do clients move?

choices.text: Both live; freeze record edits; DHCP hands out the new server; the old one keeps answering until its log goes quiet
choices.why: Rung 2: a temporary replica. The forum answer gives the same advice: keep both running for a while, so clients that have not moved still get DNS and you can roll back.

choices.text: Swap the addresses in one step at midday
choices.why: A rung 7 step with no way back, while everyone is working.

choices.text: Hand out both servers and keep editing records on whichever is handy
choices.why: Pi-hole's FAQ says devices may use either listed server, so the order is no priority. Without a freeze, clients get two different answers.

choices.text: A night window with a straight swap
choices.why: It works, but it spends downtime the parallel run does not need.

steps.situation: The old Pi-hole also serves DHCP. When does that move?

choices.text: Last, in a short announced window: off on the old, then on on the new; re-enable the old to roll back
choices.why: Rung 7, prepared. The forum answer: never two DHCP servers, and turning DHCP back on at the old one is the rollback.

choices.text: Enable DHCP on both for an overlap
choices.why: Two DHCP servers on one network hand out conflicting leases and options.

choices.text: Leave DHCP on the old box for good
choices.why: It works today, but the box you meant to retire stays a single point of failure.

steps.situation: Every client has moved and the old server's log is quiet. What now?

choices.text: Add a second resolver, keep settings pinned, schedule an export off the box, lift the freeze and say so
choices.why: Teach: one DNS server was the single point of failure for everything, including image pulls.

choices.text: Wipe the old box the same hour
choices.why: It was your way back. Keep it for a few days.

choices.text: Raise the rate limit and never look for the noisy client
choices.why: It hides the client as well as relieving it.

debrief.what_happened: The source thread is a plan, not a failure: on 30 April 2025 a user asked how to move a Pi-hole v6 that also served DHCP. The answer agreed with the plan and added two rules: run old and new side by side for a while so unmoved clients keep DNS and rollback stays possible, and never run two DHCP servers; turning DHCP back on at the old one is the way back. Pi-hole's docs supply the rest: the FAQ says clients may use either listed server; the config reference puts the per-client limit at 1000 queries per 60 seconds, answered REFUSED, and warns that listening mode ALL can make an open resolver; settings set by environment variable become read-only. A 2022 forum thread shows FTL stopping when Docker's 64 MB /dev/shm filled. In a 2025 thread a v6 server warned that eth0 did not exist on an ens18 machine; setting the interface fixed it (cause unconfirmed). The decision shape follows a real migration runbook.
lessons: With no replica, build one for the length of the move.
Import data, not machine settings; pin those explicitly.
A server list is not a priority order: freeze records while two resolvers are live.
Move DHCP last, in a window, never two servers at once.
